narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 65.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the single strongest reason the model expected you to struggle. Being in the bottom decile that year strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile, added further weight in the same direction, though less dramatically. These two performance signals outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70 worked in the opposite direction. It was the only notable factor that pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. However, because it was well below the 3.23 average of accepted students, its helpful effect was limited and could not overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 32, middle family income, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in law school. Stronger grades and higher rankings in the coming years can meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. Consider academic support resources now so you can build the record that will demonstrate your readiness for the bar exam.
